text: Each account is a name followed by a list of emails. Two accounts belong to the same person if they share at least one email. Merge them and return, per person, the name followed by all their emails in sorted order.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — merging is driven purely by shared emails, and the name is only there for output. Two different people could share a name but stay separate if they share no email. Is that right?
Correct — shared email is the only link.

Let me run through the example. Two John accounts both contain johnsmith, so they merge into one John with johnsmith, john newyork and john zero zero. A separate Mary, and a third John with only johnny bravo, stay on their own. Three groups out.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. This problem reminds me of Union-Find, because grouping sets that share elements is exactly what it's built for. The key move is to make the emails the nodes, not the accounts. I give every distinct email an integer id, and within each account I union its emails together. Because the same email string always maps to the same id, any two accounts that share an email get pulled into the same set automatically. Then I bucket emails by their root, sort each bucket, and prepend the owner's name.

Here's the plan. One: map every email to an id, and record the email and its owner for each id. Two: for each account, union its first email with each of the rest. Three: bucket every email under its root, sort each bucket, and put the owner's name in front. One thing worth flagging — I union in a star: the first email links to each of the rest, which is linear in k per account, not the k squared of connecting every pair. And a subtle indexing point — the mapping loop starts at i equals one, so every email, including a lone one, gets registered, while the union loop starts at i equals two, since the first email is the star center. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Find and Union are the usual size-based Union-Find. The first loop gives each new email the next id and records its owner. Then I size parent to the number of distinct emails, run the star unions, bucket each id under its root, and for each bucket sort it and insert the owner of the root at the front. One thing worth flagging — registering emails in the first loop from i equals one is what makes single-email accounts like Mary show up at all. They never get a Union, but they still get an id and a bucket.

Let's dry-run on the example. I'll shorten the emails to smith, N Y, J zero zero, mary, and bravo, with ids zero to four. The row that matters is the second John account: smith already has id zero, so Union of zero and two pulls J zero zero into the same set as N Y. Mary and bravo get no union and stay alone. So the roots are zero, three and four — three groups. John gets J zero zero, N Y, smith, in sorted order. The two Johns that never shared an email stayed separate — just as the clarification predicted.

Let N be the total number of emails. The union and find work is N times inverse Ackermann, effectively linear. The bottleneck is sorting the buckets — across all groups that's N emails, so N log N overall. Space is linear, for the map, the parent array, and the buckets. Oh, one more thing — the same shape solves with plain DFS: build a graph where each account star-links its emails, then flood-fill each component. Union-Find is just tighter here, and it's the same core as counting components or finding a cycle edge — only the nodes changed from integers to email strings.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You made emails the nodes, so shared emails merge for free. You used a star union to stay linear per account. And you nailed that the name is output-only — two same-name accounts with no shared email stay separate. Good work.
